title: Durable execution and checkpoints
summary: Long agent runs must keep their state outside the process, so a crash, deploy or long wait resumes from the last checkpoint instead of restarting. Checkpoints help you resume. Durable execution adds retries, timers and deterministic replay.
useIf: A run lasts hours, waits for humans, calls flaky tools or must survive restarts and deployments.
avoidIf: A run lasts seconds to minutes and restarting from scratch is cheap and safe. A plain in-process loop is simpler.

explain.md: A checkpoint is a saved snapshot of run state. In Agent Framework workflows, checkpoints are written at the end of each superstep and capture executor state, pending messages, pending requests and responses and shared state. C# uses `CheckpointManager`, and from Python 1.13.0 an entry checkpoint is also written before the first superstep and when responses to request events arrive [[r21]]. LangGraph checkpointers store thread-scoped state for human-in-the-loop, time travel and fault tolerance. Its `interrupt()` needs a checkpointer and a `thread_id`, and waits indefinitely until resumed with `Command`; `InMemorySaver` loses state on restart, and old checkpoints should be pruned [[r43]][[r44]].

explain.title: Resume instead of restart
explain.alt: Each step persists a checkpoint before the next step. After a crash or restart the run loads the latest checkpoint and continues from the next step.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  S[Run step] --> P[(Persist checkpoint)]
  P --> N[Next step]
  N --> S
  X[Crash or deploy] --> L[Load latest checkpoint]
  L --> N

explain.md: **Durable execution** goes further. Temporal runs code as durable execution: workflow code must be deterministic because it is replayed, side effects live in Activities with retry policies, timeouts and heartbeats, and timers can last months [[r42]]. The Durable Extension for Agent Framework offers durable agents, multi-agent orchestrations and checkpointed workflows on Azure Functions or your own compute, in C# and Python (Go listed as coming soon), using Durable Task infrastructure such as the Durable Task Scheduler. Human-in-the-loop waits consume no compute and no model tokens, so a 24-hour approval costs only seconds of execution on Flex Consumption. Its install uses a prerelease flag (`--prerelease` for .NET packages, `--pre` for pip), and the page states no GA status, so check before promising production use [[r12]].

Anthropic's production lessons are the same shape: agents are stateful and errors compound, so resume from where the agent was, combine model-level error handling with retries and regular checkpoints, and deploy with rainbow deployments so old and new versions run together while traffic shifts [[r2]]. Its Managed Agents design separates an append-only session log, the harness and the sandbox, so a new harness can resume with `wake(sessionId)` (beta, header `managed-agents-2026-04-01`) [[r15]]. For API-level asynchrony, OpenAI background mode runs a response asynchronously that you poll or cancel, and without `store=true` the data is kept only about 10 minutes [[r25]].

explain.title: A checkpoint is not exactly-once
explain.md: Resuming from a checkpoint can repeat a step whose side effect already happened. Pair checkpoints with idempotency keys or compensating steps, and keep orchestration code deterministic when replay is used.

whereToUse: Workflows that wait for human approval for hours or days
Agents that call flaky or rate-limited tools and need retries with backoff
Systems deployed continuously while runs are in flight
Pipelines where partial progress is expensive to redo

use: Runs last longer than a typical deploy or timeout
A human or external system may take hours to respond
Tool failures are common and restarts are expensive
avoid: Short, cheap runs where restarting is safe
Teams without capacity to operate a durable runtime, unless a managed option fits
Treating in-memory checkpoint savers as durable
flips: Waits grow from minutes to days: move to a durable wait that costs no compute
Side effects cannot repeat: add idempotency keys and compensations
Preview or unverified GA status blocks adoption: use framework checkpoints with your own store and test recovery

pitfalls.symptom: All progress is lost after a restart
pitfalls.cause: State lived in memory, or the checkpoint saver was in-memory
pitfalls.fix: Persist state to a durable store and test a kill-and-resume drill.

pitfalls.symptom: A resumed run sends the same message twice
pitfalls.cause: The step completed before the crash but its checkpoint was not written
pitfalls.fix: Use idempotency keys on side effects and record completion before acting where possible.

pitfalls.symptom: Replay produces a different path than the original run
pitfalls.cause: Non-deterministic code, such as time or random values, runs inside replayed orchestration [[r42]]
pitfalls.fix: Move side effects and non-determinism into activities and keep orchestration code deterministic.

pitfalls.symptom: A deploy breaks runs in flight
pitfalls.cause: Old runs resume on incompatible new code
pitfalls.fix: Version workflows, or use rainbow deployments so old and new run side by side [[r2]].

scenarios.title: Six-hour run with flaky tools
scenarios.situation: A data-processing agent runs for about six hours and calls external tools that fail roughly one call in twenty. The service redeploys several times a day, and restarting from scratch costs a lot.
unknowns: Can the team operate a durable runtime?
scenarios.question: Where does the run live?

options.name: Durable orchestration or checkpointed workflow with retries, versioned or rainbow deploys and idempotent activities
options.why: It resumes after crashes and deploys, retries failing calls with policy and keeps side effects safe.
options.tradeoff: Determinism rules, operations effort and a status check on the runtime you choose.

options.name: In-process loop with a retry wrapper
options.why: Every deploy or crash discards hours of work.
options.tradeoff: Right for short runs where a restart is cheap.

options.name: Framework checkpoints in a local in-memory saver
options.why: Cheap to add and handles some failures.
options.tradeoff: An in-memory saver loses state on process restart, so it fails the deploy case.

flips.then: An in-process loop with a simple retry is enough.

flips.if: The durable runtime is preview and policy forbids it
flips.then: Use framework checkpoints with a durable store you operate.

scenarios.takeaway: Longer than a deploy means state must live outside the process.

scenarios.title: Short runs, cheap restart
scenarios.situation: A support agent finishes in under a minute. Tools are idempotent reads, and an interrupted run can be retried by the user. The team is small.
constraints: Retry by the user is acceptable
scenarios.question: Do you add durable execution?

options.name: Keep an in-process loop with step cap, timeout and a user-visible retry
options.why: The cost of failure is tiny, so durable infrastructure would cost more than it saves.
options.tradeoff: An interrupted run restarts from scratch.

options.name: Adopt a durable orchestration platform
options.why: It adds operational weight and determinism rules for no benefit here.
options.tradeoff: Right once runs grow to hours or approvals appear.

options.name: Persist checkpoints to a database after every step
options.tradeoff: Added storage, schema and complexity before it is needed.

flips.if: Tools start writing to external systems
flips.then: Add idempotency keys first, then consider checkpoints.

scenarios.takeaway: Do not buy durability that the failure cost does not justify.

quiz.q: When are Agent Framework workflow checkpoints written?
options: At the end of each superstep
quiz.explain: Checkpoints are written at the end of each superstep and capture executor state, pending messages, pending requests and responses and shared state. Python 1.13.0 added entry checkpoints as well. [[r21]]

quiz.q: After a restart, a resumed run repeats a paid API call. Which changes address it?
options: Send an idempotency key with the call
Switch the checkpoint saver to in-memory
Record completion before acting, or use a compensating step
quiz.explain: Idempotency keys and completion records or compensations make repeats safe. An in-memory saver loses state and a larger step cap does nothing for duplicates. [[r26]][[r27]]

flashcards.back: A checkpoint lets a run resume. Durable execution adds retries, timers and deterministic replay, with side effects in activities [[r42]].
A checkpointer and a thread_id. It waits indefinitely until resumed with Command. InMemorySaver loses state on restart [[r44]][[r43]].

flashcards.front: Why do durable human-in-the-loop waits cost little?
flashcards.back: They consume no compute and no model tokens while waiting. A 24-hour approval costs seconds of execution on Flex Consumption [[r12]].
